transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brought you in to see me today?

I called the EAP because I’ve been jumping at every little noise in the office. A file drawer shuts or somebody drops a mug, and I jump really hard. Then my chest keeps racing for way longer than it seems like it should.
Did these symptoms start after any particular stressful or frightening event happened to you, or did they come on gradually without a clear trigger?
Yeah. It started about two weeks ago, after this late-night confrontation with my regional boss.
Since that night, have you been having unwanted, vivid memories or flashbacks of the confrontation popping into your mind when you don't want them to?
No, I haven’t really had memories of it popping back up like that.
Since that night, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or situations that remind you of the confrontation?
I haven’t really noticed myself avoiding anything because of it.
Since this started, has the jumpiness and racing heart been significant enough to interfere with your ability to concentrate at work or manage your usual daily activities?

I’m still getting to work, but I’m slower with accounts and staffing decisions. I’ve had to ask my team to double-check things I’d normally handle myself. With performance reviews coming up, I’m worried the mistakes could affect my job.
Can you tell me more about what happened during that confrontation with your boss—did it involve any threats of violence, harm, or feel life-threatening in any way?
I’m not sure what you mean. It was a confrontation, but I don’t really know how to answer whether it was life-threatening.

Do you notice these jumpy, racing-heart episodes mainly when something reminds you of that night with your boss, or do you feel keyed up and anxious pretty much throughout the day regardless of what's happening around you?
Mostly at the office. I keep checking where my boss is, where the exits are, and whether anyone’s coming up behind me, even when I’m supposed to be focused on my team.
During that confrontation, did your boss threaten you physically, raise a hand, or make you fear for your safety in any way, or was it entirely a verbal disagreement about work matters?
I don’t know. I mean, it was a confrontation, but I’m not really sure how to put it in terms of whether I feared for my safety.

During that confrontation, did your boss do anything specific—like get physically close, block your path, throw or hit something, or make any statement that made you think you might be physically harmed—or was it entirely shouting and heated words about work issues?
I honestly can’t say there was a specific thing like that. I remember it being really tense and heated, but I’m not sure I can describe it any more clearly than that.
During that confrontation, did you personally feel, even briefly, that you might be seriously hurt or that your life was in danger?
I’m not sure I’d say I thought I was going to be seriously hurt or killed. It was very tense, but I can’t honestly say I felt my life was in danger.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient developed hyperarousal symptoms (exaggerated startle response, racing heart, hypervigilance about exits/boss's location) within two weeks of a discrete interpersonal stressor (a heated confrontation with his boss) that does not meet Criterion A for PTSD/ASD, as he explicitly denies any threat of death, serious injury, or fear for his safety/life during the event. He also denies intrusive re-experiencing symptoms (flashbacks) and avoidance behaviors, which argues against PTSD or Acute Stress Disorder. The anxiety symptoms are clearly time-linked to the identifiable stressor, occur predominantly in the context reminiscent of that stressor (the office/boss), and are causing clear functional impairment (decreased work performance, need for double-checking, worry about upcoming performance reviews). This pattern—emotional/behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor, causing impairment, without meeting full criteria for another anxiety or trauma-related disorder—is most consistent with Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety.
